p.x:
Last weekend was great! On Saturday afternoon, I went to the cinema with my best friend, Lek. We wanted to watch a horror film, but Lek is afraid of scary films, so we watched a comedy instead. The main actor was very funny, and the whole audience laughed a lot.
On Saturday evening, my brother and I went to a concert in the park. A famous band from Bangkok played their new songs. The singer had an amazing voice, and the guitar player was brilliant. My brother bought their new album after the show.
On Sunday, I stayed at home. I practised the piano for an hour, then I listened to music in my room. In the evening, my family watched a film on TV together. It was a lovely, relaxing weekend.

"The Night Market" is the new film from young Thai director Pim Siriwat, released in cinemas this month. The plot follows Nok, a shy student who sells noodles at a Bangkok night market to pay for university. One night, she meets an old man who claims he can see the future, and her life changes completely.
The cast is excellent. Newcomer Ploy Arun gives a natural, believable performance as Nok, and every character, from the noisy market sellers to Nok's strict mother, feels real. The best scene comes near the end, when Nok has to perform a song at a talent show in front of the whole market.
The soundtrack is also a highlight. It mixes traditional Thai instruments with modern pop, and the lyrics of the final song are beautiful. If I have one complaint, it's that the middle part of the film is a little slow; it sometimes feels like an episode of a TV series. Overall, though, this is an entertaining and touching film. My review score: four stars out of five.

Twenty years ago, if you wanted to watch a new film, you went to the cinema or waited months for it to appear on DVD. Today, streaming platforms release thousands of films and series instantly, and audiences can watch them on any device. This has changed not only how we watch, but also what gets made.
One effect has been the rise of international content. Thanks to subtitles and dubbing, Korean dramas, Spanish thrillers and Thai horror films now find global audiences. Critics have praised several of these productions, and some acclaimed series have become worldwide hits. Viewers have discovered that a captivating story can cross any language barrier.
However, streaming has also changed the economics of the industry. Studios increasingly prefer safe investments: sequels, remakes and adaptations of famous books or video games, which come with a ready-made audience. Original films in less popular genres struggle for funding, and a young director's debut may never reach a cinema at all.
Meanwhile, cinemas focus on the big blockbuster experience that can't be recreated at home. Actors, too, notice the difference: some say the long rehearsal periods of the past have been replaced by fast production schedules designed to feed an endless demand for content.
